Description: The surviving upper half of a gypsum slab inscribed with a summary inscription of the Assyrian king Adad-nirari III (reigned 811-783 BC). Found at Nimrud (ancient Calah) in 1854 by William Loftus, the slab was then lost and only relocated in 1993 in the Upper Chambers; for over a century scholars knew it only from a squeeze made by Edwin Norris. Its text lists lands subdued and made tributary, including Tyre, Sidon, Edom, Palastu (Philistia), and Humri - the Assyrian name for the land of Omri, that is, Israel.
Interpretations: The slab names Israel (as Humri, 'land of Omri') among the western lands brought under Assyrian dominance in the early 8th century BC, matching the biblical picture of a weakened Israel under Aramean pressure. Scholars widely identify Adad-nirari III as the 'deliverer' of 2 Kings 13:5, though the Bible does not name him; that identification is strong but inferential, not stated in the text.
BiblicalSignificance: It places Israel on the Assyrian record a generation before the fall of Samaria, and gives a historical face to the unnamed 'deliverer' God raised up for Israel in 2 Kings 13:5.
CurrentLocation: Unknown (last recorded in the Upper Chambers at Nimrud, 1993)
